source_title: Howard Zinn, A People's History of the United States, ch. 7 'As Long as Grass Grows or Water Runs' (libcom.org full-text mirror)
source_cite: Zinn, People's History, ch. 7
source_quote: Treaties made under pressure and by deception broke up Creek, Choctaw, and Chickasaw tribal lands into individual holdings, making each person a prey to contractors, speculators, and politicians.
notes: Quote matches the chapter text exactly (print page not seen; mirror has no pagination). Zinn's next sentences say the Chickasaws 'sold their land individually at good prices and went west without much suffering' while 'great numbers' of Creeks and Choctaws were 'defrauded by land companies', so the fraud claim applies to Creek and Choctaw, not Chickasaw. Zinn cites Van Every (9 mentions), Rogin (6), Foreman (1). Instrument cites are atlas cites, consistent with local STAT-7-366 and STAT-7-333. Zinn is a non-Native synthesizer; cite Saunt/Haveman and the treaty text for map flags.

source_title: Andrew Jackson, Letter to the Creek Indians, March 23, 1829 (American Presidency Project); Zinn ch. 7

source_quote: you can live upon it, you and all your children, as long as the grass grows or the water runs, in peace and plenty. It will be yours for ever.
corrected_summary: Zinn's chapter title quotes Jackson's 1829 instructions for the Choctaws and Chickasaws (the 'army major' talk): land 'which they shall possess as long as Grass grows or water runs.' The Creek letter of March 23, 1829 says 'you can live upon it, you and all your children, as long as the grass grows or the water runs, in peace and plenty. It will be yours for ever.' The row's quoted wording ('They can live upon it, they and all their children...') matches neither verified text; it may be the Oct. 15, 1829 Haley draft, which could not be reached. Zinn does not discuss the Curtis Act or Indian Territory allotment; the 'broken within a generation' link is the atlas's own inference.
corrected_instrument_cite: Jackson, Letter to the Creek Indians, Mar. 23, 1829 (presidency.ucsb.edu); Jackson to David W. Haley, Oct. 15, 1829, draft (Papers of Andrew Jackson, UTK; not reached)
notes: Zinn's version: 'There, beyond the limits of any State, in possession of land of their own, which they shall possess as long as Grass grows or water runs.' thepapersofandrewjackson.utk.edu did not resolve from this sandbox; the Haley draft wording is unresolved. Display the Creek letter text (verified) rather than the row's paraphrase.

source_title: Howard Zinn, A People's History, ch. 1 'Columbus, the Indians, and Human Progress' (libcom.org mirror)
source_cite: Zinn, People's History, ch. 1
source_quote: One reason these atrocities are still with us is that we have learned to bury them in a mass of other facts, as radioactive wastes are buried in containers in the earth.
corrected_summary: Zinn's ch. 1 reframes 1492 through Las Casas and the people he calls 'Arawaks' (current usage: Taino), and argues that historians such as Samuel Eliot Morison mention the genocide but bury it 'in a mass of other facts' (Morison's 'complete genocide' line is 'on one page, buried halfway into the telling of a grand romance'). He does not say 'in footnotes.' The critique of Zinn (few Native-authored sources, victim framing, selective use of Morison) is from secondary reviews and was not checked against named reviewers here.
notes: Ch. 1 mentions Las Casas 10 times, Arawak 12, Koning 1, Morison several times (verified). The limits/critique part is the atlas's characterization; if displayed, attribute to a named reviewer (e.g., Michael Kazin, Dissent 2004; not checked this pass).

source_title: Treaty with the Creeks, Mar. 24, 1832, 7 Stat. 366, Arts. I, II, XII
source_cite: 7 Stat. 366, Art. I-II, XII
source_quote: The Creek tribe of Indians cede to the United States all
corrected_summary: The 1832 treaty text itself cedes all Creek land east of the Mississippi (Art. I). It then reserved one section to each of 90 principal chiefs and a half section to every other head of family, 'reserved from sale for their use for the term of five years' (Art. II), and said no Creek was compelled to emigrate: 'they shall be free to go or stay, as they please' (Art. XII). So Royce's reading of a full cession matches the text; the dispute is about what happened to the individual reserves (fraud and speculator purchases, then the 1836 war and forced removal). The 6,696 reserve count is Haveman's figure and was not checked.
notes: Quote is truncated where the OCR margin note ('by the Indians.') interrupts; Art. I continues 'their land, East of the Mississippi river.' The row's federal_account_contrast ('in text it was a guarantee of individual reserves') is contradicted by Art. I and should be rewritten. Map: show the whole area as ceded by treaty with individual five-year reserves inside it, then reserves lost to fraud (Zinn ch. 7 and Saunt support the fraud), then 1836 removal.

source_cite: Maine Wabanaki-State Child Welfare TRC, Beyond the Mandate (2015)
source_quote: Wabanaki children in Maine have entered foster care on average at 5.1 times the rate of nonNative children during the past 13 years.
corrected_summary: The report gives 5.1 times the non-Native rate for 2000 to 2013 (not 'five times' for 2002 to 2013). It states that these conditions and disproportionate entry into care 'can be held within the context of continued cultural genocide, as defined by the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide.' Root causes named: underlying racism, historical (intergenerational) trauma, and differing interpretations of tribal sovereignty and jurisdiction; the report discusses MICSA's 'possible effect on Native child welfare.' Mandate endorsed February 2013, signed by the governor and five chiefs 'as equals'; 159 statements gathered (95 Native, 64 non-Native).
notes: The report calls the Commission 'a first-in-the-nation event.' The link between MICSA and child removal is framed by the TRC as a 'possible effect', so the map should say 'the TRC links' rather than state causation.

source_title: Executive Order N-15-19 (Gov. Gavin Newsom, June 18, 2019), signed PDF
source_cite: Cal. Exec. Order N-15-19 (June 18, 2019)
source_quote: apologizes on behalf of the citizens of the State of California to all California Native Americans for the many instances of violence, maltreatment and neglect California inflicted on tribes
corrected_summary: The executive order apologizes and creates the Truth and Healing Council, and quotes Gov. Peter Burnett's 1851 address ('a war of extermination will continue to be waged between the two races until the Indian race becomes extinct'), but the order itself does not use the word 'genocide.' Newsom called it 'a genocide' in his spoken remarks that day (AP). The order set the final report for 'on or before January 1, 2025'; the Governor's office later said it would be released in 2025. Release not confirmed. The order also states it does not create any rights or benefits enforceable against the State.
notes: The apology wording ('on behalf of the citizens', 'violence, maltreatment and neglect') mirrors the 2009 federal apology (WEB-HIS-032), and the no-rights clause mirrors the 1993/2009 disclaimers: useful for the 'apology without remedy' tour. Burnett quote verified only as quoted in the EO; original is in the Journal of the Senate of California, 1851 (not checked). Check tribalaffairs.ca.gov/cthc for the final report before launch.

source_title: JCCW, 'Massacre of Cheyenne Indians' (38th Cong., 2d Sess., 1865); Doolittle Committee, Condition of the Indian Tribes (1867); Treaty of the Little Arkansas, 14 Stat. 703, Art. VI; Pub. L. 105-243, 112 Stat. 1579

Doolittle's own conclusion lists the causes of decline as disease, intemperance, wars (among themselves and with whites), white emigration that destroys game, and 'the irrepressible conflict between a superior and an inferior race'; 'cruel treatment on the part of the whites' is Gen. Pope's testimony quoted by the committee, not the committee's own finding. Little Arkansas Art. VI (14 Stat. 706) expresses US condemnation and repudiation of the 'gross and wanton outrages' at Sand Creek and grants land and reparations; the 1998 Act finds 'the United States admitted guilt and reparations were provided for in article VI... those treaty obligations remain unfulfilled' (not 'never paid to most descendants').

No. 142, 38th Cong., 2d Sess.; Doolittle report number and Jan. 26, 1867 date not confirmed in the OCR. Sand Creek coordinates not checked.

source_title: Pub. L. 103-150, 107 Stat. 1510 (Nov. 23, 1993); Hawaii v. Office of Hawaiian Affairs, 556 U.S. 163 (2009)
source_quote: Whereas the indigenous Hawaiian people never directly relinquished their claims to their inherent sovereignty as a people or over their national lands to the United States, either through their monarchy or through a plebiscite or referendum;
corrected_summary: The 'never directly relinquished' language is a preambular 'whereas' clause (107 Stat. 1512), not an operative finding. The same preamble also recites that the Republic of Hawaii 'ceded 1,800,000 acres' to the US. Sec. 3 says 'Nothing in this Joint Resolution is intended to serve as a settlement of any claims against the United States' (107 Stat. 1514). In 2009 a unanimous Court held the resolution's operative verbs are 'conciliatory or precatory', that the 37 'whereas' clauses cannot bear that weight, and that the resolution did not strip Hawaii of authority to alienate the ceded lands. The row's contrast ('Congress itself found they were never relinquished') overstates: Congress recited that Native Hawaiians never relinquished their claims.
notes: Map label suggestion stands: 'Crown and Government lands (called "ceded lands" in state and federal law).' Quote the whereas clause as a congressional recital, with the 2009 holding beside it.

source_quote: (b) Disclaimer.--Nothing in this section-- (1) authorizes or supports any claim against the United States; or
notes: Disclaimer verified; clause (2) 'serves as a settlement of any claim against the United States' follows after the 123 Stat. 3454 page break. Sec. 8113(a) begins on 123 Stat. 3453 and (b)(2) runs onto 3454. Note a further limit: the apology in (a)(4) is 'on behalf of the people of the United States' for violence, maltreatment and neglect 'inflicted on Native Peoples by citizens of the United States', not expressly by the government, though (a)(3) recognizes 'official depredations' and 'the breaking of covenants by the Federal Government'. source_title: Indian Claims Commission Act, Aug. 13, 1946, 60 Stat. 1049, secs. 2, 15, 22
source_cite: 60 Stat. 1049, sec. 2, sec. 15, sec. 22
source_quote: The payment of any claim, after its determination in accordance with this Act, shall be a full discharge of the United States of all claims and demands touching any of the matters involved in the controversy.
notes: Verified in the Act: sec. 15 caps attorney fees at '10 per centum of the amount recovered'; sec. 2 requires deductions for payments and offsets and lets the Commission consider 'funds expended gratuitously for the benefit of the claimant'; sec. 22(a) makes payment a full discharge and sec. 22(b) bars further claims after an adverse final determination. Not in the Act text (they come from ICC and Court of Claims practice, per secondary sources): money-only awards, valuation at date of taking, and no interest on non-Fifth-Amendment claims. Attribute those to Rosenthal or Lieder & Page when displayed. $1.3 billion total not checked.

source_title: Johnson v. M'Intosh, 21 U.S. 543 (1823); City of Sherrill v. Oneida Indian Nation, 544 U.S. 197 (2005); Joint Note of the Dicasteries for Culture and Education and for Promoting Integral Human Development on the 'Doctrine of Discovery' (Mar. 30, 2023)
source_cite: 21 U.S. (8 Wheat.) 543, 587; 544 U.S. 197, 203 n.1; Holy See Press Office Bulletin 230330b
source_quote: The “doctrine of discovery” is not part of the teaching of the Catholic Church.
corrected_summary: Johnson quote is accurate but Marshall phrases it as the US position the Court accepts: 'They maintain, as all others have maintained, that discovery gave an exclusive right to extinguish the Indian title of occupancy, either by purchase or by conquest' (21 U.S. at 587). Sherrill does not cite Johnson by name; its footnote 1 invokes the 'doctrine of discovery' through Oneida II (470 U.S. 226, 234) and Oneida I (414 U.S. 661, 667). The Vatican note says the doctrine is not Church teaching, that the bulls 'have never been considered expressions of the Catholic faith', and that the Church 'repudiates those concepts that fail to recognize the inherent human rights of indigenous peoples, including what has become known as the legal and political doctrine of discovery'; it does not rescind the bulls. Correct 'cited in Sherrill' to 'the doctrine was invoked in Sherrill (2005)'.
notes: Caveat for the map stands: church repudiation, not legal repudiation. The note itself says the legal concept 'found particular expression in the nineteenth century jurisprudence of courts in several countries'.
